name: Gregorio Allegri
bio:
Allegri was born in Rome around 1582 and grew up there as a choirboy at San Luigi dei Francesi, the church of the French community, where he studied with the composer Giovanni Bernardino Nanino. He was intended for the Church, and for some years he held a post at the cathedral of Fermo, in central Italy, where he wrote many motets and other sacred works.

His music came to the notice of Pope Urban VIII, and on 6 December 1629 Allegri joined the choir of the Sistine Chapel as a singer, a post he held for the rest of his life. He published collections of sacred concertos and motets, and wrote masses, settings of the Lamentations of Jeremiah and a little music for strings; one of these pieces was printed by the scholar Athanasius Kircher in his great book on music, *Musurgia universalis* (1650). He was remembered as a kind man who gave generously to the poor and to prisoners.

He died in Rome in February 1652. His fame rests almost entirely on one work, the *Miserere*, written in the 1630s for the Holy Week services of the Sistine Chapel. For generations the papal singers performed it with ornaments of their own, passed on by ear, and the music gained an aura of secrecy. The story that the fourteen-year-old Mozart wrote it down from memory in 1770 made it famous across Europe, and 20th-century recordings turned its soaring soprano line into one of the best-known sounds in choral music.

name: Ludwig van Beethoven
bio:
Beethoven grew up in Bonn, in a family of court musicians. His father, a singer, pushed him hard as a child prodigy, and in his teens Ludwig was already playing in the court orchestra and helping to support the family. In 1792 he moved to Vienna to study with Haydn, and he soon made his name there as a ferocious pianist, famous above all for his improvising.

In his late twenties he began to lose his hearing. In 1802, in a letter to his brothers now known as the Heiligenstadt Testament, he admitted that he had thought of ending his life, and that only his art had held him back. What followed was a burst of bold, large-scale works, among them the *Eroica* and the Fifth Symphony. By his last years he was almost completely deaf, yet he kept composing, and wrote the Ninth Symphony and his late string quartets.

Beethoven died in Vienna in 1827, and a huge crowd followed his funeral procession. He changed what people expected music to do: a symphony could now be a personal statement, a struggle that ends in triumph, or a deep meditation. He stretched old forms such as [[sonata-form|sonata form]] until they could hold far more drama than before. Almost every composer who came after him, from Brahms to Mahler, worked in his shadow.

portrait.title: Beethoven with the Manuscript of the Missa solemnis

name: Hector Berlioz
bio:
Berlioz was born in 1803 in La Côte-Saint-André, a small town near Grenoble, where his father was a doctor. He was sent to Paris to study medicine, but he hated the dissecting room and spent his evenings at the opera instead. Against his family’s wishes he gave up medicine for music and entered the Paris Conservatoire. Unusually for a composer, he never became a real pianist; his instruments were the flute and the guitar.

In 1827 he saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia and Juliet, and fell obsessively in love with her. That passion poured into the *Symphonie fantastique* of 1830, a piece of [[programme-music|programme music]] about an artist’s love, his opium dreams and a nightmarish witches’ sabbath, with the beloved represented by a returning melody, the [[idee-fixe|idée fixe]]. He did eventually meet and marry Harriet, but the marriage was unhappy.

Berlioz thought in sound and colour, and his book on orchestration was studied by composers for generations. In France he was often misunderstood and made much of his living as a music critic, while audiences in Germany, Russia and England welcomed him as a conductor. His epic opera *Les Troyens* was never staged complete in his lifetime. He died in Paris in 1869.

name: Johannes Brahms
bio:
Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833, the son of a double-bass player who scraped a living in the city’s dance halls and theatres. Johannes was earning money at the piano while still a teenager. In 1853 he met Robert and Clara Schumann, and Robert, then one of the most respected composers in Germany, published an article hailing the twenty-year-old as the future of music.

Schumann’s praise was both a gift and a burden. Brahms worked on his First Symphony for about twenty years, all too aware of Beethoven looking over his shoulder, and it was finally premiered in 1876, when he was 43. After Robert Schumann’s death he remained devoted to Clara for the rest of her life, as friend and confidant; the exact nature of their bond is still debated.

He settled in Vienna in the 1860s and became one of the most admired figures in European music, writing four symphonies, *A German Requiem*, concertos, and a great deal of chamber music and songs. Brahms loved old forms such as the [[variation|variation]] and the [[passacaglia|passacaglia]], and filled them with warm, autumnal feeling. He died in Vienna in 1897, less than a year after Clara.

name: Anton Bruckner

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Nine numbered (the Ninth unfinished), plus two early ones

bio:
Bruckner was born in 1824 in Ansfelden, a village near Linz in Upper Austria, the eldest child of the village schoolmaster. His father gave him his first music lessons and taught him the organ. When his father died in 1837, the 13-year-old was sent to the Augustinian monastery of St Florian as a choirboy, and he was in awe of its great organ. He trained as a schoolteacher and spent his late teens and twenties teaching in village schools, playing the organ and composing on the side.

In 1848 he became organist at St Florian, and in 1855 he won the post of cathedral organist in Linz. That same year he began years of study, mostly by post, with the Viennese theorist Simon Sechter. He only started composing in earnest at 37, after lessons with the young conductor Otto Kitzler, who introduced him to the music of Richard Wagner. In 1868 he moved to Vienna to teach at the Conservatory, and as an organist he toured France in 1869 and England in 1871, where he played at the Royal Albert Hall.

His symphonies had a hard time in Vienna. Bruckner revered Wagner and dedicated his Third Symphony to him, and from then on the city’s most powerful critic, Eduard Hanslick, a champion of Brahms, treated him as a dangerous Wagnerite. The Third’s premiere in 1877 was a fiasco. Real success came only at 60, with the Seventh Symphony in Leipzig in 1884. Fiercely self-critical, he revised his scores again and again, which is why many exist in several versions. He died in Vienna in 1896 with his Ninth Symphony unfinished, and lies in the crypt of St Florian, beneath his favourite organ.

name: Frédéric Chopin

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Piano music: nocturnes, ballades, études, mazurkas, polonaises

bio:
Chopin was born in 1810 in Żelazowa Wola, a village west of Warsaw, to a French father, Nicolas, who had settled in Poland, and a Polish mother. The family moved to Warsaw when he was a baby, and Polish was spoken at home. He was giving public concerts by the age of seven, and from 1826 he studied composition with Józef Elsner at the Warsaw Conservatory. In November 1830 he left to make his name abroad. A few weeks later the November Uprising broke out at home, and he never saw Poland again.

He reached Paris in 1831 and stayed for the rest of his life. He disliked large halls and gave only about thirty public concerts; he earned his living by teaching and played mostly in private salons. In 1836 he met the novelist George Sand. They were together from 1838 to 1847, spending a difficult winter on Mallorca and most summers at her country house at Nohant, where he wrote many of his finest works.

Almost everything he wrote involves the piano: nocturnes, études, ballades, preludes, scherzos, and the Polish dances, mazurkas and polonaises, that kept his homeland in his music. Often ill, he gave his last Paris concert in February 1848 and toured Britain that year. He died in Paris on 17 October 1849, aged 39, and the funeral march from his Second Piano Sonata was played at his graveside.

name: Antonín Dvořák
bio:
Dvořák was born in 1841 in Nelahozeves, a village on the Vltava north of Prague, where his father was a butcher and innkeeper. He was expected to take over the family business, but music won. He studied at the organ school in Prague, then spent years playing the viola in a theatre orchestra, which for a time was conducted by Bedřich Smetana.

Recognition came in his thirties. Brahms sat on the jury that awarded him an Austrian state grant, and he recommended Dvořák to his own publisher, Simrock, who brought out the *Slavonic Dances* in 1878 to huge success. Dvořák’s music, full of the dance rhythms and melodies of Bohemia and Moravia, made him famous across Europe, and especially in England, which he visited nine times.

In 1892 he went to New York as director of the National Conservatory of Music. There he wrote his Ninth Symphony, *From the New World*, and spent a summer among the Czech community of Spillville, Iowa. Homesick, he returned to Bohemia in 1895, later became director of the Prague Conservatory, and wrote his opera *Rusalka*. He died in Prague in 1904.

name: Joseph Haydn
bio:
Haydn was born in 1732 in Rohrau, a village in Lower Austria near the Hungarian border, the son of a wheelwright. At about eight he was sent to Vienna to sing in the choir of St Stephen’s Cathedral. When his voice broke he was dismissed, and for years he scraped a living by teaching and playing while he taught himself to compose. For a time he worked as accompanist and valet to the Italian composer Nicola Porpora, from whom, he said, he learned the true fundamentals of composition.

In 1761 he joined the household of the Esterházy princes, and from 1766 he directed their music for almost thirty years, much of the time at the remote palace of Eszterháza in Hungary. He had an orchestra, singers and an opera house at his disposal and could experiment as he liked. Cut off from the world, he later said, he was “forced to become original”. There he wrote most of his symphonies and string quartets and made both into central forms of the Classical style. He became a close friend of Mozart, and in 1792 the young Beethoven came to Vienna to study with him.

After Prince Nikolaus died in 1790, Haydn travelled to London with the concert manager Johann Peter Salomon, in 1791–92 and again in 1794–95. His twelve London symphonies were a triumph, and Oxford made him an honorary doctor. Back in Vienna he wrote the oratorios *The Creation* and *The Seasons*, and the hymn for the emperor whose tune is now the German national anthem. He died in Vienna in May 1809, while the city was occupied by Napoleon’s army. He is often called the father of the symphony and of the string quartet: he did not invent them, but he showed what they could do.

name: Gustav Mahler
bio:
Mahler was born in 1860 in Kaliště, a village in Bohemia, into a German-speaking Jewish family, and grew up in the nearby town of Jihlava. Many of his parents’ fourteen children died young, and death and loss echo all through his music. As a boy he loved folk songs and the military bands of the local barracks, sounds that later found their way into his symphonies. At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition.

He became one of the greatest conductors of his time. In 1897 he took charge of the Vienna Court Opera, having converted from Judaism to Catholicism shortly before, as the post effectively required. He was a fierce perfectionist, and his demand for fresh, meticulously rehearsed performances won him admirers and enemies in equal measure. For ten demanding years he transformed the company, and he composed in the summers, in small composing huts by lakes and in the mountains.

Mahler is said to have told Sibelius that a symphony must be like the world: it must embrace everything. His symphonies are vast, mixing folk songs, marches, birdsong and moments of deep stillness. After leaving Vienna he conducted in New York, at the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. He died in Vienna in 1911, aged 50, leaving his Tenth Symphony unfinished.

name: Felix Mendelssohn

facts.label: symphonies
facts.value: Five numbered, plus 13 early string symphonies

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Violin Concerto, *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, *Songs without Words*

bio:
Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 into a wealthy, cultured family; his grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn. The family moved to Berlin when he was two, the children were baptised as Protestants, and his parents later added the surname Bartholdy. Felix and his older sister Fanny, herself a gifted composer, grew up surrounded by music. At 16 he wrote his String Octet, and at 17 the overture to *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*.

In 1829, aged 20, he conducted Bach’s *St Matthew Passion* in Berlin, a performance that helped bring Bach’s music back into concert life. He travelled widely, to Italy and many times to Britain, and the journeys gave him the *Italian* Symphony, the *Scottish* Symphony and the *Hebrides* overture, inspired by Fingal’s Cave. In 1835 he became director of the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig, and in 1843 he founded the Leipzig Conservatory.

He worked at a furious pace as composer, conductor, pianist and organiser. His oratorio *Elijah* was first performed in Birmingham in 1846. In May 1847 his sister Fanny died suddenly, and less than six months later, on 4 November, he died in Leipzig after a series of strokes, aged 38. Later in the century his polished, light-filled music fell out of fashion, partly through antisemitism, but works such as the Violin Concerto never left the concert hall.

portrait.title: Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy
portrait.license: Public domain (Public Domain Mark, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin; artist d. 1874)

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
bio:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the son of Leopold, a violinist and composer who was also a gifted teacher. Wolfgang was writing little pieces by the age of five, and as a child he toured the courts and concert halls of Europe with his father and his older sister, Nannerl, a brilliant keyboard player herself. Those years on the road filled his ears with every musical style of the day, from Italian opera to German counterpoint.

In 1781 he broke with his employer, the Archbishop of Salzburg, and settled in Vienna as a freelance musician, a rare and risky move at the time. He earned his living by teaching, playing his own piano concertos at subscription concerts and selling his music. The Vienna years brought *The Marriage of Figaro*, *Don Giovanni* and *The Magic Flute*, and his last three symphonies, all written within a few weeks in the summer of 1788.

He died in Vienna in December 1791, aged 35, with his *Requiem* unfinished; his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it. What lasts is the feeling that nothing in his music is forced. Melodies that sound effortless turn out to be carefully built, and even the brightest pages can cloud over in a bar or two. That is why his music works on a first hearing and still rewards the hundredth.

name: Sergei Rachmaninoff

facts.label: bestKnownFor
facts.value: Piano Concertos Nos. 2 and 3, *Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini*

bio:
Rachmaninoff was born in 1873 into a landowning family in the Novgorod region of north-west Russia. His father’s debts cost the family its estates, and in 1882 they moved to a small flat in St Petersburg. After two unsettled years at the conservatory there, at twelve he was sent to Moscow to live with Nikolai Zverev, a strict piano teacher who took in a few pupils as boarders. He graduated from the Moscow Conservatory in 1892 with the Great Gold Medal. His student opera *Aleko* won Tchaikovsky’s praise, and his Prelude in C-sharp minor soon made his name far beyond Russia.

In 1897 the premiere of his First Symphony was a disaster, and for three years he wrote almost nothing. Treatment with the physician Nikolai Dahl helped him back to work, and the Second Piano Concerto (1901), dedicated to Dahl, became his most popular piece. The years that followed were full: in 1902 he married his cousin Natalia Satina, he conducted at the Bolshoi Theatre, he spent three winters in Dresden, where he wrote his Second Symphony, and in 1909 he toured America with his Third Piano Concerto, written for that tour.

The Russian Revolution ended that life. In December 1917 he left Russia with his family and never returned. To support them he became a touring pianist, one of the greatest of his time, and settled in the United States. He composed much less, partly in a villa he built on Lake Lucerne, where he wrote the *Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini* (1934). His last work was the *Symphonic Dances* (1940). He died in Beverly Hills on 28 March 1943, four days before his seventieth birthday.

portrait.license: Public domain (PD-Bain, PD-old; Library of Congress, no known restrictions)

name: Franz Schubert
bio:
Schubert was born in Vienna in 1797, the son of a schoolmaster. As a boy he sang in the choir of the imperial court chapel, which came with a place at a boarding school, where he played in the student orchestra and had lessons with Antonio Salieri. For a few years he taught at his father’s school, but what he really did was write music, at an astonishing rate.

He never held an important post, and he was never famous in the way Beethoven was, though they lived in the same city. Instead he had a devoted circle of friends, who gathered for evenings of his music that came to be called Schubertiades. He wrote more than 600 songs, among them *Erlkönig*, composed when he was 18, and the song cycle *Winterreise* (“Winter Journey”).

He fell seriously ill in his mid-twenties and died in 1828, aged just 31. Much of his greatest music, including the *Unfinished* Symphony and the *Great* C major Symphony, was only performed in public years after his death. His gift was melody, but also mood: in Schubert, a sudden change of key can feel like a cloud passing over the sun.

name: Robert Schumann
bio:
Schumann was born in 1810 in Zwickau, in Saxony, the son of a bookseller and publisher, and he grew up loving literature as much as music. He went to university in Leipzig and Heidelberg to study law, but he soon gave it up for the piano and lessons with Friedrich Wieck, a famous teacher in Leipzig. A weakness in the fingers of his right hand, whose cause is still uncertain, ended his hopes of a career as a pianist, and by 1832 he had turned to composing.

In 1834 he helped to found a music journal, the *Neue Zeitschrift für Musik*, and for ten years he wrote much of it himself, often signing as two imaginary characters: fiery Florestan and dreamy Eusebius. Through the 1830s he wrote mostly piano music, such as *Carnaval* and *Kinderszenen*. He fell in love with Wieck’s daughter Clara, already a celebrated pianist; her father fought the match in court, and they married only in September 1840. That year he poured out songs, including the cycle *Dichterliebe*, and in 1841 he turned to symphonies.

In 1844 the family moved to Dresden, and in 1850 to Düsseldorf, where he became the city’s music director. In 1853 the twenty-year-old Brahms called on the Schumanns, and Robert hailed him in print as a genius. Soon afterwards his mental health collapsed. In February 1854 he threw himself into the Rhine, was rescued, and spent his last two years in an asylum at Endenich, near Bonn, where he died in 1856, aged 46. Clara outlived him by forty years and kept playing his music throughout her long career.

portrait.title: Robert Schumann
portrait.license: Public domain (PD-Art, PD-old-100-1923; lithograph, artist d. 1876)

name: Dmitri Shostakovich
bio:
Shostakovich was born in St Petersburg in 1906. After his father died, the teenager helped support the family by playing the piano in cinemas, accompanying silent films. He studied at the Petrograd Conservatory, and his First Symphony, written as a graduation piece when he was 19, made him famous almost overnight; within a few years it was being played in Berlin and in the United States.

His life was bound up with Soviet politics. In 1936 the Communist Party newspaper *Pravda* attacked his opera *Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District* as “muddle instead of music”, a dangerous charge at the height of Stalin’s purges. He answered in 1937 with his Fifth Symphony, which was greeted with a long ovation. In 1948 he was denounced again, and for years he kept some of his most personal works in a drawer.

During the Second World War his Seventh Symphony, the *Leningrad*, became a symbol of resistance; in 1942 it was even performed in the besieged city itself. He wrote fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets, music that can be savagely ironic one moment and desolate the next. People still argue about what his music was trying to say, which may be part of its power. He died in Moscow in 1975.

name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
bio:
Tchaikovsky was born in 1840 in Votkinsk, a factory town in the Urals where his father managed the ironworks. His family steered him towards a safe career: he trained in law and worked as a clerk at the Ministry of Justice in St Petersburg. In his early twenties he began to study music seriously, and he was among the first students of the new St Petersburg Conservatory.

In 1866 he moved to Moscow to teach harmony at the conservatory there. Success came gradually, with the First Piano Concerto, the ballet *Swan Lake* and the opera *Eugene Onegin*. A wealthy widow, Nadezhda von Meck, paid him an allowance for thirteen years that let him compose full time, on condition that they never meet. His brief marriage in 1877 was a disaster: Tchaikovsky was gay, at a time when that had to be hidden.

By the 1880s he was the first Russian composer whose music was celebrated internationally, and he conducted his work in Leipzig, London and New York, where he took part in the opening of Carnegie Hall in 1891. He died in St Petersburg in 1893, nine days after conducting the premiere of his Sixth Symphony, the *Pathétique*. The official cause was cholera, and it is still argued over.
